Hansen ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0001-8630-2875 1 , Josh Erickson 2 , Max Lindmark ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-3841-4044 3 , Luke McPhan 4 , 5 , 6 , Paul Humphries 6 , 7 & … Eva Bergman ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0003-2220-1615 1 Show authors Nature Water ( 2026 ) Cite this article Save article View saved research Abstract The River Wave Concept is a theoretical interpretation of river ecosystem processes that links flow to multiple river ecosystem concepts and contextualizes how a river functions with or without anthropogenic impacts. Here we propose a framework that can map the River Wave Concept to ecosystem concepts and wave metrics using widely available flow data from gauging station networks. The framework can produce a three-dimensional River Wave visualization, a time series of ecosystem process changes over time and wave metrics that can be related to organism patterns across space. Our case study contrasted Sweden’s fragmented rivers with modelled free-flowing conditions and found that the observed fragmented rivers may favour specific fish life history strategies, that ecosystem functioning has shifted towards more baseflow-dominated flow compared with free-flowing rivers and that restoring all rivers to free-flowing conditions would result in more similar rivers nationally. Our study highlights how river theory can help to identify river ecosystem change and provide data to inform new analyses, which are critical for managing impacts on rivers. Ecosystem ecology Hydrology Ecological Dynamics of Riverine Systems Main River ecosystems are experiencing an exceptional decline in biodiversity because of anthropogenic impacts and climate change 1 , 2 , 3 . This decline is a direct consequence of human alterations to a river’s natural flow regime 4 . Changing a river’s natural flow regime results in cascading changes to a river’s hydrological, geomorphological, biogeochemical and ecological processes 5 . To manage these ecosystems effectively, a variety of river ecosystem concepts (also referred to as theories or models) help to explain these processes in relation to one another. Here, three concepts are most important: (1) the river continuum concept, which focuses on the gradient of energy and resources from source to mouth of a river 6 ; (2) the flood pulse concept, which emphasizes the lateral connectivity of energy and resources between the main channel and its floodplain; and (3) the riverine productivity model, which focuses on local and in-stream production provided by local energy and resources 7 . Although these concepts have shaped our understanding of river ecology for decades 8 , they remain conceptually disjointed. Each one of them often focuses on specific types of river 9 (for example, temperate, near-pristine and forested headwater streams) or assumes a single particular dimension of a river ecosystem (for example, longitudinal, lateral, vertical or temporal) 10 , limiting their transferable utility. Furthermore, it is unclear how to interpret and apply these concepts when most river flow patterns around the world are altered by dams 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 . For river managers and policymakers, this conceptual misalignment creates a critical disconnect between ecological theory and management practice. Resolving this gap requires a unified conceptual framework that integrates these disparate ecosystem concepts, using hydrological flow as the primary organizing variable to address a broader spectrum of contemporary river challenges. The River Wave Concept (hereafter referred to as River Wave) was proposed to unify the river continuum concept, the flood pulse concept and the riverine productivity model via flow while also incorporating anthropogenic alterations 15 . By reframing river discharge as a physical wave—defined by its intensity, amplitude, wavelength and frequency—the River Wave indicates that the original river ecosystem concepts are not competing ideas but rather distinct ‘functional states’ that occur at different positions on the wave. The novelty of this idea is that it enables analysis of the area under a hydrograph and the shape of a hydrograph to jointly provide a conceptual link between raw flow measurements and the river processes they help to explain. For example, as a hydrograph rises and falls over time, the area under this curve helps determine which concept is most appropriate for a river (for example, the river water level enters the floodplain, which indicates the flood pulse concept), whereas the shape of the line helps to determine the potential ecological response (for example, a peak flood event triggers fish spawning). Despite its potential to inform a broad range of river ecosystem processes, the River Wave has remained largely theoretical, due to a lack of quantitative tools to map its concepts onto real-world hydrological data.
